theme: Temptation, the Fall, the curse, and the first gospel promise
settingTheScene: Yesterday we saw the world as it was meant to be: a garden, a man, a woman, work and rest, presence and partnership, no shame. Today everything changes. Genesis 3 is the story of how the very good creation of chapters 1 and 2 was broken. But more than that, it is the chapter that explains every news headline, every funeral, every estrangement, every disease, every disordered desire you have ever experienced. The whole biblical story of redemption assumes Genesis 3. Without this chapter, the gospel makes no sense, because without this chapter, there is nothing for the gospel to fix.
observation: The serpent does not begin with a direct contradiction. He begins with a question: “Did God actually say…?” Doubt is planted before disobedience.
Eve’s response slightly distorts God’s command, she adds “neither shall you touch it.” The slightest drift from God’s actual word makes further drift easier.
The serpent finally contradicts God directly: “You will not surely die.” He then accuses God of withholding something good, “you will be like God.”

The order of the temptation is striking: the woman saw that the tree was good for food (the appetite), a delight to the eyes (the senses), and to be desired to make one wise (the mind). 1 John 2:16 echoes this triad.
Adam was “with her.” He was not deceived in the same way; he failed in passive silence.

Their first response to sin is shame, they suddenly know they are naked and try to cover themselves. Their second is hiding from God. Their third is blame, Adam blames the woman (and implicitly God for giving her), the woman blames the serpent.
Verse 15 is the first gospel promise: the offspring of the woman will crush the serpent’s head. Before any curse is even spoken to humanity, a promise of victory is given.
God himself clothes them with garments of skin, the first death in Scripture is an animal slain to cover human shame.
interpretation:
Genesis 3 is the most consequential chapter in the entire Old Testament. Everything in human experience that you grieve, every relational wound, every body that breaks down, every system that goes wrong, finds its origin here. And yet, before the chapter ends, the gospel has already been promised. This is both the worst news in Scripture and the moment when the best news begins.

The temptation is subtle. The serpent does not roar in declaring God a liar; he whispers a question. “Did God actually say…?” Doubt always precedes rebellion. Notice what is being attacked: not God’s existence, not even God’s power, but God’s word. If God’s word cannot be trusted, if it is unclear, or stingy, or designed to keep us from something better, then disobedience starts to feel reasonable. The serpent’s whole strategy is to make God seem less generous than he is. He frames God’s one prohibition as if it were God’s whole posture: “Did God actually say you shall not eat of any tree?” But God had said the opposite, eat of every tree, except this one. Generosity comes first, prohibition is the exception. The serpent inverts it.

Eve’s response begins well but slips. She defends God’s generosity, but then she adds something God never said: “neither shall you touch it.” It is a small drift, but every great failure begins with a small drift from God’s actual word. The serpent then makes his move. He flatly contradicts God (“you will not surely die”) and slanders God’s motives (“God knows that when you eat of it your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God, knowing good and evil”). The accusation is that God is holding out on them, that obedience keeps them from their true potential.

And here is the heart of all sin: the desire to define good and evil for ourselves, to be like God on our own terms. Eve’s eyes go to the fruit. It is good for food, pleasing to look at, and seems to offer wisdom. Three categories of desire are activated, appetite, beauty, ambition, and she takes. The Hebrew word translated “took” is the same word later used for taking another man’s wife or seizing what is not yours. It is the language of theft. And Adam, who has been “with her” through the whole exchange, takes too, in silence.

What happens next is the world we now live in. Their eyes are opened, but not to be like God. They are opened to shame. They cover themselves with leaves. They hide from God when he comes walking in the garden. When God confronts them, they blame, Adam blames Eve, and implicitly God himself (“the woman whom you gave to be with me”); Eve blames the serpent. Sin always fractures relationships. With God, with each other, with creation itself.

Then come the curses. The serpent is cursed first. The woman’s pain in childbearing and her relationship with her husband are disordered. The man’s work, once a joy, will now be filled with thorns and sweat. And finally death, “to dust you shall return.” The full weight of God’s earlier warning falls. But there, in the middle of the cursing of the serpent, comes verse 15: “I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your offspring and her offspring; he shall bruise your head, and you shall bruise his heel.” This is the protoevangelium, the first gospel. Before any judgment is pronounced on humans, before any human is sent out of the garden, a promise has already been made: a son of the woman will one day come and crush the serpent’s head. The cost will be real, the serpent will bruise his heel. But the victory belongs to the woman’s offspring.

And then, in a quiet act of mercy, God makes garments of skin and clothes Adam and Eve. Animals die to cover human shame, the first hint of a sacrificial principle that will run through the entire Bible, all the way to a cross where the Lamb of God will bear the sin of the world.
connection: Yesterday’s covenant of works has been broken. The man and woman who were placed in the garden as priest-king and partner have failed the test, and the consequences fall on themselves, their children, and the creation entrusted to them. But the story does not end with the curse. Genesis 3:15 is the seed from which every later promise grows, the promised offspring of Abraham, the suffering servant of Isaiah, the son of David, the Word made flesh. When Romans 16:20 says God will “soon crush Satan under your feet,” it is echoing Genesis 3:15. When Christ on the cross declares “It is finished,” he is fulfilling Genesis 3:15. The whole Bible is the unfolding of the promise made in this chapter, that the seed of the woman would do what Adam failed to do, and would crush the head of the one who deceived humanity.
application:
Look at the serpent’s strategy and recognize it, because it is still in use today. “Did God actually say…?” The accusation that God is withholding something good. The framing of obedience as oppression and disobedience as liberation. These are the same temptations you will face this week, this year, your whole life. The defense is not stronger willpower. The defense is a settled trust in God’s word and God’s character. The serpent could not have succeeded if Eve had said: “Whatever God said, he said because he is good. I do not need to be like God; I am made by God, and that is enough.”

Today, consider one place in your life where you are tempted to think God is holding out on you. Maybe it is a desire you are being asked to wait on or set aside. Maybe it is a command that feels restrictive. Bring it before God honestly. And then remember that the very God who gave that command is the God who, in this same chapter, made the first promise of a Savior, and who, in the fullness of time, sent his only Son to crush the serpent and clothe sinners not in leaves but in his own righteousness. Your trust in God’s word and your trust in God’s love are not separable. Trust both today.
readingInstruction: Read Genesis 3:1-24 slowly, and aloud if you can. This is the saddest chapter in the Bible and the most important for understanding everything that follows. Notice what the serpent asks, how Adam and Eve respond, and how God appears in the story, both in judgment and in promise (look closely at verse 15).
prayerPrompts: Confess in your own words where you have listened to the serpent’s doubt about God’s word or goodness.
Thank God for the promise of the one who would crush the serpent, and tell him what that means to you.
Ask him to clothe you in Christ rather than in your own coverings.
